Optimized Neuro-Adaptive Third-Order Sliding
Mode Control With High-Gain Di ﬀerentiator for
Enhanced Photovoltaic System Performance:
Simulation and Experimental Validation
Ameen Ullah
 , Safeer Ullah
 , Umair Hussan
 , Baheej Alghamdi, and Jianfei Pan, Member , IEEE
Abstract—This article addresses the challenge of optimizing
photovoltaic (PV) system performance under rapidly changing
environmental conditions, such as ﬂuctuations in solar irra-
diance and temperature. To enhance energy extraction and
regulate power delivery, a noninverting dc–dc buck–boost con-
verter is employed. Motivated by the nonlinear behavior and
uncertainty inherent in PV systems, we propose a novel con-
trol strategy—neuro-adaptive third-order sliding mode control
(NATOSMC)—that ensures accurate and robust reference track-
ing. The control scheme integrates a radial basis function neural
network (RBFNN) for generating the reference signal, and a
high-gain di ﬀerentiator (HGD) to estimate system states using
diﬀerential ﬂatness theory. To ensure optimal performance, adap-
tive laws adjust the control gains in real-time, with parameter
optimization performed via the gray wolf optimizer (GWO).
Stability is rigorously guaranteed through Lyapunov analysis.
Both simulation and experimental results validate the proposed
method, demonstrating superior performance in terms of track-
ing precision, dynamic response, and robustness compared to
conventional controllers. Key results include a settling time of
0.014 s, rise time of 0.012 s, overshoot of 0.05%, and tracking
eﬃciency of 98.71%. The controller also achieves improved
performance indices: integral of absolute error (IAE) of 111.04,
integral square error (ISE) of 11 .42 × 105, integral time absolute
error (ITAE) of 3.19, and integral time square error (ITSE) of
1.21 × 104. These results highlight the e ﬃcacy of NATOSMC
in enhancing the control and reliability of PV energy systems.
Index Terms —High-gain di ﬀerentiator (HGD), maximum
power extraction, photovoltaic (PV) system, radial basis function
neural network (RBFNN), third-order sliding mode control
(SMC).

I. I NTRODUCTION
T
HE economic growth of a nation is closely associated
with the robustness of its energy infrastructure. Although
oil and gas have long been central to global energy con-
sumption, their widespread use has resulted in signiﬁcant
environmental damage. The increasing dependence on fossil
fuels has contributed to increased harmful emissions, worsen-
ing global warming, and climate change. As the world grapples
with the challenges of sustainable development, it is crucial
to explore cleaner energy options and reduce reliance on
pollution sources to ensure a sustainable future. The increasing
demand for electrical energy is driven by factors such as
industrial expansion; population growth; and the increasing
prevalence of technological systems, devices, and machinery
that consume large amounts of energy [1]. Renewable energy
sources have emerged as the most promising solution for
addressing these evolving energy needs while minimizing
environmental harm [2]. Major forms of renewable energy
include solar power [3], wind energy [4], green hydrogen
[5], and hydropower [6]. In contrast to nonrenewable energy
sources such as natural gas, these sources are favored for their
abundance and ease of use.
Among the various renewable energy sources, wind, and
solar energy have emerged as the most extensively adopted
because of their cost-e ﬀectiveness, environmental sustain-
ability, and minimal carbon footprints [7]. These renewable
resources play a vital role in addressing the increasing global
electricity demand, while simultaneously reducing reliance on
conventional fossil-fuel-based energy production. Solar energy
is harnessed through photovoltaic (PV) cells, while wind
turbines are used to convert kinetic wind energy into elec-
trical power [8]. It is essential to recognize the fundamental
diﬀerences between wind and solar energy systems in terms
of their operational principles, technological concepts, and
core components. This study focuses on electricity generation
through PV systems, emphasizing their potential as a sustain-
able solution for energy production. Governments worldwide
increasingly support PV technology, as they provide a reli-
able and eco-friendly alternative for generating electricity.
Moreover, PV systems often include battery storage to e ﬀec-
tively manage surplus energy, ensuring continuous power
availability during periods of low solar irradiance or high
demand [8].

PV systems are a relatively recent advancement in elec-
trical systems, demonstrating a high capacity for electrical
energy generation compared with various other technologies.
Many governments recognize this system as a key option for
enhancing energy yield through advanced technology. In a
PV system, solar energy is transformed into electrical power
using multiple panels, each equipped with thousands of PV
cells [9]. These cells are responsible for generating electric
current. The system is noted for its simplicity, absence of toxic
emissions, low maintenance requirements, cost-e ﬀectiveness,
ease of operation, and longevity, which often exceeds 25
years [10]. Furthermore, PV systems contribute signiﬁcantly to
environmental protection and mitigate risks to bird migration
routes, unlike wind energy systems, which utilize turbines
[11]. By utilizing PV systems, households and businesses
can reduce their reliance on expensive grid electricity, poten-
tially lowering or eliminating electricity bills. To promote
the adoption of PV technology, many governments provide
incentives and credits, which can help alleviate the initial
installation costs. A key challenge for PV systems is the
requirement to store surplus energy produced during daylight
for nighttime use, which involves additional equipment and
expenses. This issue is typical among renewable systems
dependent on variable sources, such as solar and wind, owing
to the current limitations and high cost of energy storage
technologies. In addition, the performance of PV systems is
inﬂuenced by weather conditions, leading to ﬂuctuations in
energy production based on the time of day and environmental
factors [4].
PV system performance is typically evaluated using
power–voltage ( P–V) and current–voltage ( I–V) charac-
teristics, which exhibit nonlinear behavior inﬂuenced by
environmental variations [12], [13]. These variations com-
plicate the extraction of maximum power, necessitating the
use of MPPT techniques [14]. MPPT algorithms are designed
to ensure PV systems consistently operate at their optimal
power output, thereby improving e ﬃciency. Various meth-
ods have been proposed to enhance MPPT performance,
including conventional perturb and observe (P&O) [15],
improved P&O [16], incremental conductance (INC) [17],
and its enhanced versions [18]. Other advanced strategies
involve fractional-order PI (FOPI) control [19], [20], sliding
mode control (SMC) [21], neural networks [22], fuzzy logic
control (FLC) [23], [24], fuzzy SMC (F-SMC) [25], and
super-twisting SMC (STSMC) [26]. Each approach di ﬀers
in complexity, robustness, sensor requirements, and cost. For
instance, SMC demands accurate system modeling, which
may hinder practical implementation. Conversely, the hybrid
FLC–particle swarm optimization (PSO) method presented
in [27] demonstrated improved tracking performance and
dynamic response, though it introduced additional complexity.
Overall, the selection of an MPPT method involves tradeo ﬀs
between performance and implementation feasibility.
In [28], a P&O MPPT strategy with variable step size was
implemented using an Arduino Mega, achieving improved
maximum power point (MPP) tracking with reduced oscil-
lations compared to conventional ﬁxed-step P&O. This
adaptation enhances system responsiveness, reduces power
ﬂuctuations, and improves current quality. Another advanced
MPPT method, detailed in [29], combines INC with a
neuro-fuzzy variable step size to optimize power output
under varying environmental conditions. This hybrid approach
minimizes power ripples, enhances dynamic response, and
improves e ﬃciency over standard methods. In a related
improvement, Awan [30] introduced an enhanced P&O algo-
rithm using a “decrease and ﬁx” technique to accelerate
tracking speed by stabilizing step size adjustments. By ana-
lyzing voltage and current data, this approach e ﬀectively
distinguishes power changes due to perturbations from those
caused by weather variations, reducing power ripples and
enhancing current quality. Similarly, Yilmaz et al. [31] pro-
posed an FLC for MPPT to handle ﬂuctuating weather
conditions, integrating a proportional–integral (PI) controller
and a buck converter for e ﬃcient battery charging. This
approach, which replaces the PI controller with an FLC, boosts
system robustness under varying irradiation and temperature,
improving power stability and current quality compared to tra-
ditional control. Finally, Ahmad et al. [32] presented an MPPT
strategy based on a fractional-order PI–derivative (FOPID)
controller. Designed for simplicity and cost-e ﬀectiveness, this
approach enhances system response, reduces disturbances in
output voltage, and improves power stability relative to con-
ventional techniques.
The study presented in [33] introduced an advanced SMC
method tailored to improve the robustness and e ﬃciency of
MPPT systems operating under dynamic environmental condi-
tions. This modiﬁed SMC strategy incorporates an innovative
sliding surface designed to reduce chattering e ﬀects, resulting
in a more e ﬃcient and durable MPPT solution compared to
conventional techniques. Similarly, Derri et al. [34] proposed
an F-SMC approach that enhances the extraction of the
MPP by minimizing oscillations around the operating point.
This method improved the overall e ﬃciency of PV systems
by reducing power ripples and improving current quality.
Despite its durability and e ﬀectiveness, the F-SMC approach
is associated with increased complexity, higher costs, and
challenges in implementation. Furthermore, Shahdadi et al.
[35] introduced an optimized SMC strategy to achieve MPPT
using a dc–dc SEPIC converter. This method demonstrated
signiﬁcant improvements in the robustness of PV systems,
enabling them to perform e ﬀectively under varying envi-
ronmental conditions and system uncertainties. Collectively,
these studies underscore the potential of advanced SMC-based
techniques to enhance MPPT performance, even in challenging
real-world scenarios.
Terminal SMC (TSMC) has attracted considerable interest
due to its ﬁnite-time convergence and strong robustness in
nonlinear systems [36], [37]. In [38], a TSMC strategy was
optimized using PSO to enhance PV system performance,
enabling accurate MPPT under varying environmental con-
ditions. The PSO-tuned parameters improved robustness and
reduced oscillations compared to conventional TSMC. Sim-
ilarly, Tariba et al. [39] applied an integral SMC (ISMC)
technique, achieving faster dynamics and better MPPT perfor-
mance than traditional PI controllers across diverse climates.
These nonlinear control methods notably improve the dynamic

In [40], a second-order SMC (SOSMC) method incorporat-
ing a super-twisting algorithm was used for MPPT, o ﬀering
fast response and reduced chattering under varying environ-
mental conditions—outperforming traditional SMC. However,
the added complexity of SOSMC presents implementation
challenges. Similarly, Guo et al. [41] proposed a robust
SOSMC scheme for grid-connected PV systems using a
voltage-source inverter, focusing on sinusoidal current delivery
and reduced total harmonic distortion (THD), with improved
robustness against parameter variations. Despite its advan-
tages over conventional PI controllers, complexity remains a
limitation. In [42], an SOSMC-based MPPT approach was
introduced with independent consideration of charge types,
enhancing resilience to disturbances. A hybrid SMC and
fractional-order SMC (FOSMC) technique was presented in
[43] for wind energy systems with PMSGs, improving dc-
link voltage regulation, power quality, tracking accuracy, and
disturbance rejection. Despite its performance, the imple-
mentation complexity of SOSMC-based methods remains
a concern. A dual-mode SOSMC strategy implemented on
OPAL-RT was proposed in [44] to regulate power and dc-
link voltage in grid-connected PV systems, demonstrating
robust and e ﬃcient performance under both normal and fault
conditions. To enhance wind power extraction, a second-
order fast TSMC (SO-FTSMC) method was introduced in
[45], o ﬀering high e ﬃciency, rapid dynamics, and minimal
voltage ﬂuctuation. Backstepping-based MPPT strategies have
also been explored. In [46], the approach showed improved
eﬃciency but at the cost of higher system complexity. Non-
linear integral backstepping was employed in [47] for dc
microgrid-based PV systems with energy storage, improving
current quality and durability while increasing cost. Similarly,
Arsalan et al. [48] proposed a backstepping controller with
integral action, enhancing power and current quality. Intel-
ligent control techniques have also gained traction. In [49],
a fuzzy-neural MPPT method with evolutionary algorithms
achieved fast dynamics and strong robustness. A mathematical
model and simulation analysis were presented in [50], con-
ﬁrming performance improvements. Finally, Roy et al. [51]
combined SMC with an integral terminal strategy to
signiﬁcantly enhance PV system e ﬃciency and control
performance.
Nonlinear control strategies have demonstrated their e ﬀec-
tiveness in enhancing the performance of PV systems,
particularly through the application of SMC. However, tradi-
tional SMC methods are often plagued by negative chattering
issues, which can compromise power quality and limit their
application. To address these challenges, a novel nonlinear
approach known as TOSMC has been introduced [52]. This
strategy has shown superior results in wind energy applica-
tions, particularly regarding energy ripples and current quality
improvements compared to conventional methods [53], [54].
One of the primary advantages of TOSMC is its simplicity
and robustness, along with its cost-e ﬀectiveness and ease

of adjustment. Unlike traditional SMC, TOSMC does not
rely heavily on the mathematical formulation of the system
under consideration, allowing it to remain relatively unaﬀected
by variations in system parameters. In addition, TOSMC is
straightforward to implement [52], [53]. Given these numerous
beneﬁts, TOSMC is employed in this study to enhance the
eﬃcacy of the PV system and mitigate its inherent challenges.
This research introduces an innovative MPPT control
methodology designed to optimize the performance of PV
systems integrated with a dc–dc buck–boost converter, as
depicted in Fig. 1 under ﬂuctuating environmental conditions,
such as variations in solar irradiance and temperature. The
main contributions of this article are summarized as follows.
1) A novel neuro-adaptive third-order SMC (NATOSMC)
scheme is proposed for PV systems, combining the
robustness of third-order SMC with the adaptability of
a radial basis function neural network (RBFNN).
2) A high-gain di ﬀerentiator (HGD) is incorporated to
estimate unmeasurable states based on system ﬂat-
ness, enhancing dynamic performance and reducing
chattering.
3) The gray wolf optimizer (GWO) is employed to opti-
mally tune control parameters, ensuring fast convergence
and robust performance under varying environmental
conditions.
4) A comprehensive Lyapunov stability analysis is con-
ducted to validate the stability and robustness of the
proposed control strategy.
5) Extensive MATLAB /Simulink simulations and exper-
imental validations are performed, demonstrating the
superiority of the proposed controller over conventional
techniques (PID, P&O, FOSMC, SOSMC, and stan-
dard TOSMC) in terms of tracking accuracy, dynamic
response, e ﬃciency, and resilience to environmental
ﬂuctuations.

B. Third-Order SMC
This section introduces an innovative MPPT control
methodology, speciﬁcally designed to enhance the e ﬃciency
and robustness of PV systems, leveraging the adaptive third-
order SMC (ATOSMC) framework. The ATOSMC algorithm
oﬀers signiﬁcant advantages over conventional SMC methods,
addressing common limitations such as chattering while main-
taining superior tracking precision and stability in nonlinear
systems.
Traditional SMC approaches have demonstrated e ﬀective-
ness in achieving rapid and reliable control in dynamic systems
[66]. However, they are often accompanied by undesirable
steady-state oscillations, commonly referred to as chattering,
which can compromise system performance and hardware
longevity [67]. To mitigate this drawback, various advanced
techniques have been developed, including TSMC [68], neu-
rofuzzy SMC [69], F-SMC [70], and high-order SMC [71].
Among these, high-order SMC methods, such as SOSMC,
have proven to be e ﬀective in reducing chattering while
improving control robustness, as evidenced in their application
to MPPT in PV systems [40].
In response to the dynamic environmental conditions expe-
rienced by PV systems, the TOSMC algorithm emerges as a
promising MPPT solution due to its ease of implementation,
adaptability to system dynamics, and minimal reliance on
precise mathematical models. Compared to FOSMC, SOSMC,
and TOSMC, ATOSMC oﬀers a streamlined approach to ﬁne-
tuning dynamic responses, enhancing energy extraction, and
ensuring rapid adaptation to environmental variations. Conse-
quently, this study employs an ATOSMC-based controller, an
enhanced version of the super-twisting algorithm, to improve
energy conversion e ﬃciency and reduce ripple e ﬀects in the
PV system.

V. C ONCLUSION
This study presents a novel MPP tracking control strategy
based on a di ﬀerentiator-driven NATOSMC framework. By
integrating an RBFNN for reference voltage generation and a
High-Gain Observer for accurate state estimation, the proposed
method achieves robust and precise tracking of the MPP
in standalone PV systems under ﬂuctuating environmental
conditions. The adaptive control law ensures real-time tuning
of controller gains, while the GWO ﬁne-tunes key parameters
to enhance tracking e ﬃciency and dynamic response further.
Comprehensive MATLAB/Simulink simulations and hardware
validations conﬁrm the superiority of the proposed controller
over traditional MPPT methods such as PID, P&O, FOSMC,
SOSMC, and standard TOSMC. The NATOSMC framework
achieves 98.71% tracking accuracy, 98.05% e ﬃciency, and a
settling time of just 0.014 s. Error performance metrics are also
improved, with IAE = 111.04, ISE = 11.42 × 105, ITAE =
3.19, and ITSE = 1.21 × 104. The controller demonstrates
strong robustness, reduced chattering, and high adaptability to
environmental variations, making it well-suited for real-world
PV applications. The versatility of the proposed approach also
makes it a promising candidate for other nonlinear and under-
actuated electro-mechanical systems, such as wind energy
systems, robotics, and electric vehicles, where similar control
challenges exist.
Future work will focus on three main directions: 1) devel-
oping alternative sliding surfaces and hybrid control archi-
tectures to further reduce chattering and enhance e ﬃciency;
2) integrating advanced machine learning techniques for real-
time optimization; and 3) conducting extended experimental
validations under impulse disturbances, step variations, and
modeling uncertainties to more thoroughly evaluate the robust-
ness and generalizability of the NATOSMC framework across
diverse operational scenarios.
